newsitem.title: USA: Dlr collapses by US close after hitting 39-mo high.
newsitem.headline: Dlr collapses by US close after hitting 39-mo high.

text.p: The dollar collapsed after surging to a 39-month high against the mark as dealers booked profits ahead of a European finance ministers' meeting and due to rumors Europe's plans to further unify could be delayed.

The U.S. unit briefly soared to 1.7423 marks -- its highest level since February 1994 -- after jobs reports in the United States and Germany highlighted the sharply divergent economic paths of the two powerhouses.
However, the dollar rally soon reversed as speculative traders who had previously bought dollars cashed in profits.

"European leaders have a meeting on Sunday and people want to square up before this meeting. People have been long, very long, lately and no one wants to be long over the weekend," said Hans Boman, chief spot dealer at Swedbank in New York.
The dollar closed near its session lows, falling to 1.7245/50 marks from 1.7375/85 at the open and 114.33/43 yen from 115.86/91.
Also spurring dollar sales was market talk that a delay would be announced at the Sunday ECOFIN gathering in Europe's plan to launch a single currency, to be called the euro, at the start of 1999.

"The dollar hasn't yet fully played out the increased possibility of a delay. It is vulnerable to retrace some of the gains it saw earlier in the week against the mark," said Bob Lynch, currency strategist at Banque Paribas in New York.

The dollar's slide escalated shortly after the U.S. midday as the rumor of a delay announcement grabbed hold of the market and dragged the dollar below significant technical levels which triggered stop-loss selling.
"The dollar just collapsed. We've broken down very quickly," said James Powers, a vice president at Westdeutsche Landesbank, as the dollar bottomed out at 1.7220 marks.
Dealers found little solace in European officials' insistance that the euro would meet its 1999 launch date.

European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said on Friday that monetary union would go ahead on time. And German Finance Minister Theo Waigel reiterated on Friday that Germany would meet the budget deficit target required for membership into the single currency and said that no talk of an EMU delay had surfaced in Bonn.
Earlier in the day, weak German jobs data led some to question Germany's ability to meet the strict fiscal criteria.

Figures from the German Bundesbank showed 11.4 percent of Germans were out of work in May, compared with 11.2 percent in April, while the U.S. jobless rate unexpectedly fell to 4.8 percent in May, its lowest level since October 1973.
Stocks and bonds rallied as the drop in the U.S. unemployment rate will likely put pressure on the Federal Reserve to tighten interest rates at its next meeting in July, underpinning the dollar.
But a weaker-than-expected 138,000 rise in May payrolls, while counteracted by upward revisions to the March and April figures, caused some to question the need for higher rates.

"You could talk a bit that the number was neutral for Fed policy, but with stocks and bonds so strong, I don't think you can get a whole lot out of that argument," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd in Chicago.
The British pound partially recovered by the U.S. close from overnight weakness despite a 25 basis point rise in UK interest rates to 6.50 percent.
Sterling closed higher at $1.6315/25 from $1.6215/25 at the open but below Thursday's close of $1.6340/50.
The dollar slipped to 1.4492/02 Swiss francs from 1.4595/05 and rose to Canadian $1.3835/40 from C$1.3795/00. The Australian dollar held steady at $0.7605/10 from $0.7606/11.
((-- Roanne Daniels, 212-859-1677))
